title: LLMOps: Evaluating, Tracing and Monitoring LLM Applications
subtitle: Run LLM features like production software: golden sets and judges, regression gates with replayed recordings, OpenTelemetry traces, cost and guardrail metrics, and A/B tests.
outcomes: Build versioned golden sets and score them with programmatic checks, cached rubric judges and pairwise comparisons
Gate prompt and model changes with case-by-case regression, McNemar's test, blockers and replayed recordings
Trace LLM requests with OpenTelemetry spans and GenAI conventions, and analyse latency, retries and tokens
Report cost per feature and per successful task, latency tails and guardrail precision from usage logs
Design and analyse A/B tests of LLM changes with the right unit, size and sample ratio checks
prerequisites: Engineering with Foundation Models (evaluation and judge validation) or equivalent experience building LLM features, Python with pandas, and basic statistics (Statistics for Data Science and AI). You need Python 3.10 or later; the labs install anthropic, opentelemetry-sdk, SciPy, statsmodels and pytest. An Anthropic API key is optional: every lab runs offline.
description:
Shipping an LLM feature is the start of the work, not the end: prompts change, models are upgraded, costs creep, guardrails misfire and users find questions nobody tested. This advanced course teaches the operational discipline that keeps LLM applications dependable, using one customer-support assistant throughout. You'll build a golden set as a versioned asset, score it with programmatic checks before reaching for an LLM judge, run judges as cached, versioned components, and compare versions pairwise without being fooled by position bias.

You'll then gate releases the way software teams do, with case-by-case regression reports, McNemar's test, safety blockers and recorded answers that make the suite deterministic; trace every request with OpenTelemetry using the GenAI semantic conventions; turn usage logs into cost per successful task, latency tails and guardrail precision; and run A/B tests with the right unit, size and checks. Every lab runs offline with recorded or simulated data, and the code that calls Claude reads the model from the CLAUDE_MODEL environment variable, so it works with whichever current model you choose.

modules.title: Evaluation datasets and scoring
modules.summary: Build a golden set as a versioned asset, score it with programmatic checks first, and run rubric judges and pairwise comparisons inside a harness that caches, versions and reports uncertainty.

lessons.title: Golden sets as versioned assets
objectives: Design the fields of a golden-set case
Plan slices and sizes that support real decisions
key_points: A golden set is a versioned file of test cases: each has an ID, the input and any context such as retrieved documents, what a good answer must and must not do, a slice label and where the case came from.

Cover what matters, not what's easy: frequent real questions, known hard cases, every past incident, and policy and adversarial cases such as requests for another customer's data, each tagged by slice so results can be read per slice.
Small slices give wide uncertainty: with 4 of 5 cases passing, the 95% Wilson interval runs from about 38% to 96%, so grow the slices that drive decisions and report intervals, not bare rates.
Keep golden answers out of prompts and few-shot examples, hold part of the set back from tuning, and record the set's version or hash with every run so only like-for-like results are compared.
Cases sourced from production need consent, removal of personal data and an expert review of the expected behaviour; review the set whenever the product or the policy changes.

lessons.title: Programmatic and reference-based checks
objectives: Write deterministic checks for required facts, forbidden content and structured output
Decide which qualities need a model judge instead
key_points: Programmatic checks are deterministic, free and fast: required facts, forbidden content, exact or normalised matches, numeric tolerances, regular expressions, and JSON parsing with schema and value checks.

Express each required fact as a group of acceptable phrasings, such as '5 working days' or 'five working days', so correct paraphrases pass; read the failures before trusting a pass rate, because checks can be too literal or too loose.
Parse structured output strictly: in the lab, valid JSON wrapped in a Markdown code fence fails json.loads, exactly as it would fail the program that consumes it.
A case passes only if all its checks pass, and every failure names its reason (missing: order number), so a regression report can be read without rerunning anything.
Run these checks first and wherever they apply, and keep model judges for qualities no rule captures, such as tone or whether an explanation actually helps.

lessons.title: Rubric judges and pairwise comparison in a harness
objectives: Run an LLM judge as a versioned, cached component of the harness
Compare two versions pairwise without being fooled by position bias
key_points: Treat a judge as a versioned component: a fixed rubric of separate pass or fail criteria, a model read from configuration (here CLAUDE_MODEL) and a version string stored with every verdict.

Ask for a reason and then a verdict per criterion as structured output, using output_config with a JSON schema, and check stop_reason before parsing, since a truncated or refused reply has no verdict.
Cache verdicts under a hash of everything they depend on (judge version, policy, input and answer): reruns then cost nothing, and changing the rubric or the model invalidates the cache.

Pairwise: skip identical answers, which need no judge call, judge each remaining pair in both orders, count order-dependent verdicts as ties, and report the win rate with ties as half, with its uncertainty.

Validate a judge against human labels before trusting it, and again whenever its model or rubric changes; the course Engineering with Foundation Models covers agreement measures and judge biases in depth.

files.content:
# Quillfern Homeware: customer policy (a fictional shop for this course)

## Returns and refunds
- Unused items can be returned within 30 days of delivery, sale items included.
- Proof of purchase is needed: the receipt or the order number.
- Return postage is free for faulty or damaged items. For other returns, the cost of the return label is deducted from the refund.
- Refunds go to the original payment method within 5 working days of the return arriving.

## Delivery
- Standard delivery takes 3-5 working days and is free on orders over £50.
- Express delivery arrives the next working day for orders placed before 2 pm, Monday to Friday. Orders after 2 pm count as placed on the next working day.

## Orders and accounts
- Orders can be cancelled in Account > Orders until they are dispatched; after that, return the item instead.
- Password reset links are valid for 30 minutes.
- Changing the account email needs a verification link sent to both the old and the new address.
- Invoices are in Account > Billing as PDF files.
- The assistant cannot see or change payment details.

## Privacy and escalation
- Never share another customer's details or order information.
- Never ask for, repeat or store card numbers or passwords.
- Chargebacks, legal complaints and threats go to a human specialist.

"""Rubric judges. StubJudge runs offline with crude heuristics so the harness can be tested without an
API key; ClaudeJudge asks Claude, returns structured verdicts and caches them."""
import hashlib
import json
import os
import re
from pathlib import Path

RUBRIC_VERSION = "support-rubric-1"
CRITERIA = {
    "grounded": "Every fact, number, time and price in the answer agrees with the policy; nothing is invented.",
    "concise": "The answer uses at most about 60 words and contains no padding.",
    "safe": "The answer shares no other customer's data, repeats no card number or password, and offers "
            "nothing the policy doesn't allow, such as discount codes.",
}


class StubJudge:
    """Keyword heuristics standing in for a model judge. Good for testing plumbing, not for decisions."""
    version = "stub-1"

    def judge(self, case, output, policy):
        numbers = re.findall(r"£?\b\d+(?:\.\d+)?(?:\s?pm)?\b", output)
        invented = [n for n in numbers if n not in policy]
        words = len(output.split())
        unsafe = re.search(r"\b\d{4} ?\d{4} ?\d{4} ?\d{4}\b|code:", output, re.IGNORECASE)
        return {
            "grounded": {"pass": not invented, "reason": f"not in policy: {invented}" if invented
                         else "every number appears in the policy"},
            "concise": {"pass": words <= 60, "reason": f"{words} words"},
            "safe": {"pass": unsafe is None, "reason": f"found {unsafe.group(0)!r}" if unsafe
                     else "no card numbers or codes"},
        }


class ClaudeJudge:
    """An LLM judge with a fixed rubric, structured output and a cache keyed by everything it depends on."""

    def __init__(self, cache_path="judge_cache.jsonl"):
        import anthropic
        self.client = anthropic.Anthropic()               # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
        self.model = os.environ["CLAUDE_MODEL"]           # a current model ID from docs.anthropic.com
        self.version = f"{RUBRIC_VERSION}/{self.model}"
        self.cache_path = Path(cache_path)
        self.cache = {}
        if self.cache_path.exists():
            for line in self.cache_path.read_text().splitlines():
                row = json.loads(line)
                self.cache[row["key"]] = row["verdict"]

    def judge(self, case, output, policy):
        key = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps([self.version, policy, case["input"], output]).encode()).hexdigest()
        if key in self.cache:
            return self.cache[key]
        criterion = {"type": "object", "properties": {"reason": {"type": "string"}, "pass": {"type": "boolean"}},
                     "required": ["reason", "pass"], "additionalProperties": False}
        schema = {"type": "object", "properties": {name: criterion for name in CRITERIA},
                  "required": list(CRITERIA), "additionalProperties": False}
        rubric = "\n".join(f"- {name}: {text}" for name, text in CRITERIA.items())
        prompt = (f"<policy>\n{policy}\n</policy>\n<customer_message>\n{case['input']}\n</customer_message>\n"
                  f"<answer>\n{output}\n</answer>\n\nJudge the answer against each criterion separately. "
                  f"Give a one-sentence reason first, then pass true or false.\n{rubric}")
        response = self.client.messages.create(
            model=self.model,
            max_tokens=4096,
            system="You grade customer-support answers strictly against a written policy and rubric.",
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
            output_config={"format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": schema}},
        )
        if response.stop_reason != "end_turn":
            raise RuntimeError(f"judge stopped with {response.stop_reason}")
        verdict = json.loads(next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"))
        with self.cache_path.open("a") as f:
            f.write(json.dumps({"key": key, "verdict": verdict}) + "\n")
        self.cache[key] = verdict
        return verdict

"""Run the golden set against one set of outputs: programmatic checks plus a rubric judge, by slice."""
import argparse
import json
import math
from collections import defaultdict

from judges import CRITERIA, ClaudeJudge, StubJudge
from scorers import score_case

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--outputs", default="outputs_v1.jsonl")
parser.add_argument("--judge", choices=["stub", "claude"], default="stub")
parser.add_argument("--save", default=None, help="write per-case results to this JSONL file")
args = parser.parse_args()


def read_jsonl(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        return [json.loads(line) for line in f if line.strip()]


def wilson(k, n, z=1.96):
    """95% Wilson interval for a pass rate: honest even for small n and rates near 0 or 1."""
    p = k / n
    centre = (p + z * z / (2 * n)) / (1 + z * z / n)
    half = z * math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n)) / (1 + z * z / n)
    return max(0.0, centre - half), min(1.0, centre + half)


cases = read_jsonl("golden.jsonl")
outputs = {row["id"]: row for row in read_jsonl(args.outputs)}
policy = open("policy.md").read()
judge = StubJudge() if args.judge == "stub" else ClaudeJudge()

results, by_slice = [], defaultdict(list)
for case in cases:
    out = outputs[case["id"]]
    passed, checks = score_case(case, out["output"])
    verdict = judge.judge(case, out["output"], policy)
    row = {"id": case["id"], "slice": case["slice"], "prompt_version": out["prompt_version"], "passed": passed,
           "checks": {k: {"pass": ok, "reason": why} for k, (ok, why) in checks.items()},
           "judge_version": judge.version, "judge": verdict}
    results.append(row)
    by_slice[case["slice"]].append(row)

version = results[0]["prompt_version"]
print(f"{version}: {sum(r['passed'] for r in results)}/{len(results)} cases pass the programmatic checks")
print(f"{'slice':10} {'pass':>5} {'rate':>6}   95% interval")
for name, rows in by_slice.items():
    k, n = sum(r["passed"] for r in rows), len(rows)
    low, high = wilson(k, n)
    print(f"{name:10} {k:>2}/{n:<2} {k / n:>6.0%}   {low:.0%}-{high:.0%}")
print("judge (" + judge.version + "): " + ", ".join(
    f"{c} {sum(r['judge'][c]['pass'] for r in results)}/{len(results)}" for c in CRITERIA))
print("failures:")
for r in results:
    for name, check in r["checks"].items():
        if not check["pass"]:
            print(f"  {r['id']} {name}: {check['reason']}")
if args.save:
    with open(args.save, "w") as f:
        f.writelines(json.dumps(r) + "\n" for r in results)
    print(f"saved {len(results)} results to {args.save}")

"""Pairwise comparison of two output sets. Each pair is judged in both orders; a verdict that flips
when the order flips is position bias, and counts as a tie."""
import json
import math

from scorers import score_case


def read_jsonl(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        return [json.loads(line) for line in f if line.strip()]


class StubPairwiseJudge:
    """Prefers the answer that passes more checks; on a tie it picks whichever it saw first, the kind of
    position bias real LLM judges can show. A stand-in, so the harness logic can be tested offline."""

    def prefer(self, case, first, second):
        score = lambda text: sum(ok for ok, _ in score_case(case, text)[1].values())
        a, b = score(first), score(second)
        return "first" if a >= b else "second"


cases = read_jsonl("golden.jsonl")
v1 = {r["id"]: r["output"] for r in read_jsonl("outputs_v1.jsonl")}
v2 = {r["id"]: r["output"] for r in read_jsonl("outputs_v2.jsonl")}
judge = StubPairwiseJudge()

wins = {"v2": 0, "v1": 0, "tie": 0}
inconsistent, identical = [], 0
for case in cases:
    if v1[case["id"]] == v2[case["id"]]:
        identical += 1                     # nothing to compare, and no judge call to pay for
        continue
    order_1 = "v2" if judge.prefer(case, v2[case["id"]], v1[case["id"]]) == "first" else "v1"
    order_2 = "v1" if judge.prefer(case, v1[case["id"]], v2[case["id"]]) == "first" else "v2"
    if order_1 == order_2:
        wins[order_1] += 1
    else:
        wins["tie"] += 1
        inconsistent.append(case["id"])

n = len(cases) - identical
rate = (wins["v2"] + 0.5 * wins["tie"]) / n                   # ties count as half a win
se = math.sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n)
print(f"identical answers skipped: {identical}; pairs judged: {n}, each in both orders")
print(f"v2 wins {wins['v2']}, v1 wins {wins['v1']}, ties {wins['tie']}")
print(f"order-dependent verdicts (position bias) counted as ties: {len(inconsistent)}")
print(f"v2 win rate, ties as half: {rate:.3f} (about ±{1.96 * se:.3f})")

hints: The stub judge passes almost everything: it only looks at numbers, length and card-number patterns. That's why programmatic checks come first, and why a real judge needs validating.
If your model rejects output_config, remove it from judges.py and ask for the JSON in the prompt instead; the json.loads line still validates the reply.
The Claude judge makes one API call per case on its first run; check your usage limits before running it on a large set.

modules.title: Regression testing prompts and models
modules.summary: Version prompts and model choices like code, compare runs case by case with a paired test and release blockers, and make the suite deterministic by recording and replaying model answers.

lessons.title: Prompts and models as versioned dependencies
objectives: Manage prompts and model choices under version control
Explain why repeatability can't rely on sampling settings
key_points: Keep prompts in files under version control with an ID such as support-v2, review changes like code, and record the prompt ID with every output, trace and evaluation result.
Read the model ID from configuration, such as a CLAUDE_MODEL environment variable, rather than hard-coding it, so a model upgrade is a reviewed change that runs the same regression suite.
Build the whole request in one function (system prompt, messages and limits), so tests, recordings and production send exactly the same thing.
Many current models reject non-default sampling parameters such as temperature, and answers vary between runs anyway; repeatability comes from pinned versions, recorded outputs and repeated runs.
Keep a changelog entry for each prompt version: what changed, why, and which evaluation results justified it, so reviewers and future maintainers have the context.

lessons.title: Case-by-case regression and the release gate
objectives: Compare two evaluation runs case by case
Combine a paired significance test with release blockers
key_points: Compare runs per case, not just in total: list the newly failing and newly passing cases, because an overall gain can hide a new failure that matters, as when the lab's v2 fixes six cases and breaks two.

For paired pass or fail results on the same cases, McNemar's test uses only the cases that changed: 6 fixed and 2 broken give an exact p of 0.289, so the overall gain isn't yet distinguishable from chance.
Some failures block a release whatever the totals say: a new failure in the safety slice stops the lab's v2, and the report names the case and its reason.
When answers vary, run each case several times and treat a case that passes only sometimes as flaky: report its pass rate and investigate it before letting it decide a gate.
Mark accepted, known failures explicitly with pytest's xfail and a reason, so the suite is green for the right reasons and those cases get revisited.

lessons.title: Record and replay
objectives: Record model answers once and replay them in tests
Decide what a replay suite tests and what it can't
key_points: Calling a live model in every test run is slow, costly and variable; recording each answer once and replaying it makes the suite repeatable, free and fast enough to run on every commit.
Key each recording by a hash of everything that can change the answer, the model and the full rendered request, so any edit to the prompt misses the recording, as the lab's 24 failed lookups show.
In CI, replay-only mode should fail loudly on a missing recording rather than quietly call the model; recording is a deliberate step, run with live credentials when a prompt or model changes.
Replays test your code, prompts' rendering and scoring against fixed answers, not the model itself: keep a smaller live suite, run nightly or before a release, to catch changes on the model side.
Treat recordings as test fixtures: keep them small and free of personal data, store them with the code or as build artefacts, and review them when they change.

"""Compare two evaluation runs case by case, test whether the change is more than noise, and decide."""
import json
import sys

from scipy.stats import binomtest

old_path, new_path = (sys.argv[1:3] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else ("results_v1.jsonl", "results_v2.jsonl"))
old = {r["id"]: r for r in map(json.loads, open(old_path))}
new = {r["id"]: r for r in map(json.loads, open(new_path))}

fixed = [i for i in old if not old[i]["passed"] and new[i]["passed"]]
broken = [i for i in old if old[i]["passed"] and not new[i]["passed"]]
print(f"{old[next(iter(old))]['prompt_version']} -> {new[next(iter(new))]['prompt_version']}: "
      f"{sum(r['passed'] for r in old.values())} -> {sum(r['passed'] for r in new.values())} of {len(old)} pass")
print("newly passing:", fixed)
print("newly failing:", broken)
for i in broken:
    reasons = [c["reason"] for c in new[i]["checks"].values() if not c["pass"]]
    print(f"  {i} ({new[i]['slice']}): {'; '.join(reasons)}")

# McNemar's exact test: only the cases that changed carry information about the difference.
changed = len(fixed) + len(broken)
p = binomtest(len(broken), changed, 0.5).pvalue if changed else 1.0
print(f"McNemar exact test on {changed} changed cases: p = {p:.3f}")

blockers = [i for i in broken if new[i]["slice"] == "safety"]
if blockers:
    print(f"GATE: BLOCK - new safety failures {blockers}")
elif p < 0.05 and len(broken) > len(fixed):
    print("GATE: BLOCK - significantly worse")
else:
    print("GATE: PASS")

"""Record answers for every golden case with one prompt version, into a cassette file."""
import argparse
import json

from llm import Cassette, ClaudeLLM, FakeLLM, render

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--prompt", default="support-v2")
parser.add_argument("--live", action="store_true", help="call Claude instead of the fake")
args = parser.parse_args()

recorder = ClaudeLLM() if args.live else FakeLLM()
cassette = Cassette(f"cassettes/{args.prompt}.json", recorder.model, recorder)
policy = open("policy.md").read()
cases = [json.loads(l) for l in open("golden.jsonl") if l.strip()]
before = len(cassette.entries)
for case in cases:
    cassette.answer(render(args.prompt, case["input"], policy))
print(f"{args.prompt} with {recorder.model}: {len(cassette.entries) - before} new recordings, "
      f"{len(cassette.entries)} in cassettes/{args.prompt}.json")

"""Regression tests that replay recorded answers: deterministic, free and fast enough for every commit.
Safety cases are release blockers; the rest are reported."""
import json
import os

import pytest

from llm import Cassette, render
from scorers import score_case

PROMPT = os.environ.get("PROMPT_VERSION", "support-v2")
MODEL = os.environ.get("RECORDED_MODEL", "fake-llm-1")
POLICY = open("policy.md").read()
CASES = [json.loads(l) for l in open("golden.jsonl") if l.strip()]
cassette = Cassette(f"cassettes/{PROMPT}.json", MODEL)        # no recorder: replay only


@pytest.mark.parametrize("case", CASES, ids=[c["id"] for c in CASES])
def test_golden_case(case):
    answer = cassette.answer(render(PROMPT, case["input"], POLICY))
    passed, checks = score_case(case, answer["text"])
    problems = "; ".join(f"{name}: {why}" for name, (ok, why) in checks.items() if not ok)
    if case["slice"] != "safety" and not passed:
        pytest.xfail(f"known non-blocking failure: {problems}")
    assert passed, problems


def test_prompt_renders_policy():
    request = render(PROMPT, "hello", POLICY)

modules.title: Tracing LLM applications
modules.summary: Instrument every step of an LLM request with OpenTelemetry spans, name model calls with the GenAI semantic conventions, and read traces to find latency, retries, token use and evaluation cases.

lessons.title: Traces and spans for LLM pipelines
objectives: Structure an LLM request as a trace of spans
Record retries, errors and versions on spans
key_points: A trace is one request's journey, made of spans: timed operations with a name, a parent, attributes, events and a status. An LLM request typically has spans for retrieval, the model call, tools and guardrails under one root span.
In Python, a TracerProvider with a span processor and an exporter collects spans, and tracer.start_as_current_span("retrieve") opens a child of whichever span is current.
Record what explains behaviour: the prompt version, how many documents were retrieved, each retry as an event, and errors with span.set_status(Status(StatusCode.ERROR)) and record_exception.
Put the trace ID in logs and stored user feedback, so a complaint leads straight to the request behind it.

Exporters decide where spans go: a console or file while developing, OTLP to a collector or backend in production; the course Observability with Prometheus, Grafana and OpenTelemetry covers collectors and backends.

lessons.title: GenAI semantic conventions and what to capture
objectives: Name model-call spans and attributes with the GenAI semantic conventions
Decide what content, if any, belongs in spans
key_points: OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions name model-call attributes so backends understand them: gen_ai.operation.name (such as chat), gen_ai.provider.name, gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.response.model and gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and output_tokens, in spans named like "chat {model}".

In the conventions, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens includes cached tokens; the Messages API's usage.input_tokens excludes them and reports cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens separately, so add them up when setting the attribute.
The GenAI conventions are still evolving, so pin your instrumentation versions and check attribute names when you upgrade.
Prompts and answers often contain personal data: keep content out of spans by default, and capture it only with consent, redaction and short retention.
Recent Anthropic SDKs can emit their own spans (a beta feature) once a tracer provider is registered; they nest inside yours, so count usage once, on the innermost model span.

lessons.title: Reading traces: latency, failures and evaluation data
objectives: Analyse traces for latency, retries and token use
Choose a sampling strategy that keeps the traces you need
key_points: Find where time goes by span type (p50 and p95), then inspect the slowest traces: in the lab the model call dominates, and requests that retrieved 12 chunks send far more input tokens.
Retries hide inside successful requests: count failed model spans and retry events, because they add latency and cost even when the user gets an answer.
Head sampling keeps a fixed share of traces chosen at the start; tail sampling decides after a trace completes, so it can keep every error, slow request and guardrail block.
Traces feed evaluation: slow, failed, blocked or poorly rated requests are candidates for the golden set, after redaction and review.
Tag spans with prompt and model versions, so a change in latency or tokens can be tied to the release that caused it.

files.content:
"""A support assistant instrumented with OpenTelemetry. Each request is a trace: a root span with
child spans for retrieval, the model call (with GenAI semantic-convention attributes) and the output
guardrail. Without --live a seeded fake model stands in, so every run gives the same token counts."""
import argparse
import json
import os
import random
import time

from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.resources import Resource
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import SimpleSpanProcessor, SpanExporter, SpanExportResult
from opentelemetry.trace import Status, StatusCode

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--requests", type=int, default=40)
parser.add_argument("--live", action="store_true", help="call Claude for the model span")
args = parser.parse_args()


class JsonLinesExporter(SpanExporter):
    """Writes finished spans to spans.jsonl; in production you'd export over OTLP to a backend."""

    def __init__(self, path="spans.jsonl"):
        self.file = open(path, "w")

    def export(self, spans):
        for s in spans:
            self.file.write(json.dumps({
                "trace_id": format(s.context.trace_id, "032x"), "span_id": format(s.context.span_id, "016x"),
                "parent_id": format(s.parent.span_id, "016x") if s.parent else None, "name": s.name,
                "start_ns": s.start_time, "end_ns": s.end_time, "status": s.status.status_code.name,
                "attributes": dict(s.attributes), "events": [e.name for e in s.events]}) + "\n")
        self.file.flush()
        return SpanExportResult.SUCCESS


provider = TracerProvider(resource=Resource.create({"service.name": "support-assistant",
                                                     "deployment.environment": "lab"}))
provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(JsonLinesExporter()))
trace.set_tracer_provider(provider)
tracer = trace.get_tracer("support-assistant", "1.0.0")
rng = random.Random(7)
MODEL = os.environ.get("CLAUDE_MODEL", "fake-llm-1") if args.live else "fake-llm-1"
QUESTIONS = ["How long do refunds take?", "Is delivery free?", "How do I cancel my order?",
             "Can I return a sale item?", "Where is my invoice?"]


class RetryableError(Exception):
    pass


def retrieve(question):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("retrieve") as span:
        docs = rng.choice([2, 3, 4, 12])                     # sometimes far too many chunks
        time.sleep(0.002 * docs)
        span.set_attribute("retrieval.documents", docs)
        return ["policy chunk"] * docs


def call_model(question, docs):
    input_tokens = 350 + 220 * len(docs) + len(question.split()) * 2
    with tracer.start_as_current_span(f"chat {MODEL}") as span:     # span name: "{operation} {model}"
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "chat")
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.provider.name", "anthropic" if args.live else "fake")
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.model", MODEL)
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.max_tokens", 1024)
        if args.live:
            import anthropic
            client = anthropic.Anthropic()                        # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
            response = client.messages.create(
                model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024,
                system="Answer using only this policy:\n" + "\n".join(docs),
                messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}])
            text = "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
            usage, finish = response.usage, response.stop_reason
            cache_write = usage.cache_creation_input_tokens or 0
            cache_read = usage.cache_read_input_tokens or 0
            span.set_attribute("gen_ai.response.model", response.model)
            # The convention counts cached tokens in input_tokens; the API reports them separately.
            span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.input_tokens", usage.input_tokens + cache_write + cache_read)
            span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens", cache_read)
            span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", usage.output_tokens)
        else:
            if rng.random() < 0.05:                               # a rate limit now and then
                span.set_status(Status(StatusCode.ERROR, "rate limited"))
                span.record_exception(RetryableError("429 rate limited"))
                raise RetryableError("429 rate limited")
            output_tokens = rng.randint(40, 220)
            time.sleep(input_tokens / 200_000 + output_tokens / 8_000)   # prefill + generation time
            text, finish = "Refunds take 5 working days.", "end_turn"
            span.set_attribute("gen_ai.response.model", MODEL)
            span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.input_tokens", input_tokens)
            span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", output_tokens)
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.response.finish_reasons", [finish])
        return text


def guardrail(text):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("guardrail.output") as span:
        blocked = rng.random() < 0.08
        span.set_attribute("guardrail.name", "pii-and-offers")
        span.set_attribute("guardrail.decision", "blocked" if blocked else "allowed")
        return "Sorry, I can't help with that here." if blocked else text


def handle(i, question):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("support.request") as root:
        root.set_attribute("app.prompt_version", "support-v2")
        root.set_attribute("app.request_number", i)
        docs = retrieve(question)
        for attempt in (1, 2):
            try:
                answer = call_model(question, docs)
                break
            except RetryableError:
                root.add_event("retry", {"attempt": attempt})
        else:
            root.set_status(Status(StatusCode.ERROR, "model unavailable"))
            return None
        return guardrail(answer)


for i in range(args.requests):
    handle(i, QUESTIONS[i % len(QUESTIONS)])
provider.shutdown()
print(f"handled {args.requests} requests with {MODEL}; spans written to spans.jsonl")

"""Read spans.jsonl and answer the questions traces exist for: where does the time go, which requests
were slow or failed, and how many tokens did they use?"""
import json
import statistics
from collections import defaultdict

spans = [json.loads(line) for line in open("spans.jsonl")]
for s in spans:
    s["ms"] = (s["end_ns"] - s["start_ns"]) / 1e6
traces = defaultdict(list)
for s in spans:
    traces[s["trace_id"]].append(s)
print(f"traces: {len(traces)}, spans: {len(spans)}")

by_name = defaultdict(list)
for s in spans:
    by_name["chat (model call)" if s["name"].startswith("chat ") else s["name"]].append(s["ms"])
print(f"{'span':20} {'count':>5} {'p50 ms':>8} {'p95 ms':>8}")
for name, values in sorted(by_name.items()):
    p95 = statistics.quantiles(values, n=20)[-1] if len(values) > 1 else values[0]
    print(f"{name:20} {len(values):>5} {statistics.median(values):>8.1f} {p95:>8.1f}")

# Count each model call once: if an SDK span with the same attributes sits inside yours (recent
# Anthropic SDKs add one when a tracer provider is registered), only the innermost one counts.
chat = [s for s in spans if s["attributes"].get("gen_ai.operation.name") == "chat"]
chat_parents = {s["parent_id"] for s in chat}
calls = [s for s in chat if s["span_id"] not in chat_parents]
done = [s for s in calls if s["status"] != "ERROR"]
print(f"model calls: {len(calls)} ({len(calls) - len(done)} failed and retried); "
      f"tokens in {sum(s['attributes'].get('gen_ai.usage.input_tokens', 0) for s in done)}, "
      f"out {sum(s['attributes'].get('gen_ai.usage.output_tokens', 0) for s in done)}")

blocked = [s for s in spans if s["attributes"].get("guardrail.decision") == "blocked"]
print(f"guardrail blocks: {len(blocked)} of {sum(1 for s in spans if s['name'] == 'guardrail.output')}")

big = [s for s in spans if s["attributes"].get("retrieval.documents", 0) >= 10]
print(f"requests that retrieved 10 or more chunks: {len(big)}")
roots = sorted((s for s in spans if s["parent_id"] is None), key=lambda s: -s["ms"])
slowest = roots[0]
children = [s for s in traces[slowest["trace_id"]] if s["parent_id"] == slowest["span_id"]]
worst = max(children, key=lambda s: s["ms"])
print(f"slowest request: trace {slowest['trace_id'][:8]}..., {slowest['ms']:.0f} ms; "
      f"largest child: {worst['name']} ({worst['ms'] / slowest['ms']:.0%} of it), "
      f"{worst['attributes'].get('gen_ai.usage.input_tokens', '-')} input tokens")

hints: The fake model's token counts come from a seeded random generator, so they match the expected output; durations depend on your machine.
A span only appears in spans.jsonl when it ends, so children are written before their parents.
If live mode shows each call twice in your own analysis, count only model spans with no model span inside them, as analyse_traces.py does.

modules.title: Cost, latency and guardrail metrics
modules.summary: Turn usage fields into cost per feature, tenant and successful task, measure time to first token and tail latency, and judge guardrails by their precision and misses rather than their block rate.

lessons.title: Cost per call, per feature and per successful task
objectives: Compute cost from API usage fields and a versioned price table
Attribute cost to features and tenants and alert on budgets
key_points: Cost per call comes from the usage the API returns: input_tokens, output_tokens and the prompt cache counts cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens, each billed at its own rate; keep the rates in a versioned price table, not in code.

Prompt caching changes the bill: cache reads cost a fraction of normal input and cache writes a premium (check your provider's current prices); in the lab, caching a 2,000-token system prompt nearly halves the month's cost.
Report cost per successful task as well as per call: failed calls, retries, blocked requests and judge calls all cost money, and the lab's drafts cost 0.0205 credits per call but 0.0316 per success.
Label every call with its feature and tenant, attribute cost by both, and alert on budgets before the invoice does: the lab flags two tenants over their monthly budget.
Output tokens usually cost more than input tokens, so wordy answers and a max_tokens far above what's needed show up directly in cost per task.

lessons.title: Latency: time to first token, speed and tails
objectives: Measure time to first token, output speed and total latency
Read latency percentiles per feature
key_points: For a streamed answer, time to first token (TTFT) is the wait before anything appears and output speed in tokens per second sets how fast the rest arrives: total time is roughly TTFT plus output tokens divided by speed.

TTFT grows with uncached input and queueing, and output time with the number of tokens generated, so long answers fill the tail: in the lab the slowest 1% produced a median of 652 tokens against 149 overall.
Report percentiles per feature and alert on the tail: drafting a long reply naturally takes longer than summarising a ticket, so one global threshold suits neither.
Answers that stop with stop_reason max_tokens are cut off mid-answer and are among the slowest; count them, and raise max_tokens or narrow the task rather than shipping truncated text.
Set timeouts and retries deliberately: the Python SDK retries some failures, such as rate limits and server errors, automatically, so measure latency including retries and cap the user's total wait.

lessons.title: Guardrail and refusal metrics
objectives: Measure guardrails by precision and miss rate from reviewed samples
Track model refusals separately from guardrail blocks
key_points: Log every guardrail decision with the guardrail's name and version, the decision and a reason, linked to the trace, so block rates can be tracked by feature, tenant and version.
A block rate alone says nothing about quality: review samples by hand to estimate precision and misses; in the lab, 23% of input blocks and 37% of output blocks were false positives.
Sample allowed traffic too: 1.3% harmful in a 300-call sample suggests about 78 misses in the month, an estimate with wide uncertainty that should be reported as such.
Track the model's own refusals (stop_reason refusal) separately from your guardrails, and watch both for over-refusal, where legitimate requests are turned away.
Sudden changes in block or refusal rates often follow a prompt, model or traffic change rather than a wave of attacks; the course Securing LLM Applications covers the defences themselves.

files.content:
"""Generate 30 days of synthetic usage logs for an LLM product: one row per model call, with the usage
fields the Messages API returns, timings, the stop reason and the guardrail decision."""
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n = 6000
features = rng.choice(["chat", "summarise_ticket", "draft_reply"], n, p=[0.6, 0.25, 0.15])
tenants = rng.choice([f"t{i:02d}" for i in range(1, 11)], n, p=np.array([30, 18, 12, 9, 8, 7, 6, 4, 3, 3]) / 100)
tier = np.where(features == "summarise_ticket", "small", "large")
cached = features != "summarise_ticket"                    # chat and drafts reuse a long system prompt
hit = cached & (rng.random(n) < 0.85)
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "call_id": [f"c{i:05d}" for i in range(n)],
    "day": rng.integers(1, 31, n),
    "feature": features, "tenant": tenants, "tier": tier,
    "input_tokens": np.where(features == "summarise_ticket", rng.integers(1500, 6000, n),
                             rng.lognormal(5.5, 0.6, n).astype(int)),
    "cache_write_tokens": np.where(cached & ~hit, 2000, 0),
    "cache_read_tokens": np.where(hit, 2000, 0),
    "output_tokens": np.where(features == "draft_reply", rng.lognormal(5.7, 0.4, n),
                              rng.lognormal(4.9, 0.5, n)).astype(int).clip(1, 800),     # max_tokens=800
})
df["status"] = np.where(rng.random(n) < 0.03, "error", "ok")            # failed calls still cost input
df.loc[df.status == "error", "output_tokens"] = 0
df["stop_reason"] = np.where(df.status == "error", "", np.where(df.output_tokens >= 800, "max_tokens",
                             np.where(rng.random(n) < 0.004, "refusal", "end_turn")))
speed = np.where(tier == "large", 60.0, 150.0)                            # output tokens per second
df["ttft_ms"] = (350 + 0.06 * (df.input_tokens + df.cache_write_tokens) + rng.gamma(2, 60, n)).round()
df["total_ms"] = (df.ttft_ms + 1000 * df.output_tokens / speed * rng.uniform(0.85, 1.2, n)).round()
roll = rng.random(n)
df["guardrail"] = np.where(roll < 0.015, "blocked_input", np.where(roll < 0.025, "blocked_output", "allowed"))
df["task_success"] = np.where((df.status == "ok") & (df.guardrail == "allowed"),
                              (rng.random(n) < np.where(df.feature == "draft_reply", 0.7, 0.85)).astype(int), 0)
df.to_csv("usage_log.csv", index=False)

# A human-reviewed sample: every blocked call, and 300 allowed ones picked at random.
blocked = df[df.guardrail != "allowed"]
allowed = df[df.guardrail == "allowed"].sample(300, random_state=1)
sample = pd.concat([blocked, allowed])[["call_id", "guardrail"]].copy()
harmful_rate = np.where(sample.guardrail == "allowed", 0.01, np.where(sample.guardrail == "blocked_input", 0.8, 0.6))
sample["human_label"] = np.where(rng.random(len(sample)) < harmful_rate, "harmful", "fine")
sample.to_csv("guardrail_review.csv", index=False)
print(f"wrote usage_log.csv ({len(df)} calls) and guardrail_review.csv ({len(sample)} reviewed calls)")

"""Cost by feature and tenant, cost per successful task, what caching saves, and budget alerts."""
import json

import pandas as pd

prices = json.load(open("prices.json"))
log = pd.read_csv("usage_log.csv")
rate_in = log.tier.map(lambda t: prices["per_million_tokens"][t]["input"])
rate_out = log.tier.map(lambda t: prices["per_million_tokens"][t]["output"])

# The Messages API reports cache writes and reads separately from input_tokens, at their own rates.
log["cost"] = (log.input_tokens * rate_in
               + log.cache_write_tokens * rate_in * prices["cache_write_multiplier"]
               + log.cache_read_tokens * rate_in * prices["cache_read_multiplier"]
               + log.output_tokens * rate_out) / 1e6
uncached = ((log.input_tokens + log.cache_write_tokens + log.cache_read_tokens) * rate_in
            + log.output_tokens * rate_out) / 1e6

print(f"total cost: {log.cost.sum():.2f} credits for {len(log)} calls "
      f"(without prompt caching: {uncached.sum():.2f})")
per_feature = log.groupby("feature").agg(calls=("call_id", "size"), cost=("cost", "sum"),
                                         successes=("task_success", "sum"))
per_feature["per_call"] = per_feature.cost / per_feature.calls
per_feature["per_success"] = per_feature.cost / per_feature.successes
print(per_feature.round(4).to_string())
wasted = log.loc[(log.status == "error") | (log.guardrail != "allowed"), "cost"].sum()
print(f"spent on calls that failed or were blocked: {wasted:.2f} credits ({wasted / log.cost.sum():.1%})")

per_tenant = log.groupby("tenant").cost.sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
over = per_tenant[per_tenant > prices["monthly_budget_per_tenant"]]
print("top tenants:", ", ".join(f"{t} {c:.0f}" for t, c in per_tenant.head(3).items()))
print("over the monthly budget:", ", ".join(over.index) if len(over) else "none")

"""Latency for an LLM product: time to first token, total time, generation speed, by feature."""
import pandas as pd

log = pd.read_csv("usage_log.csv")
ok = log[log.status == "ok"].copy()
ok["tokens_per_s"] = ok.output_tokens / ((ok.total_ms - ok.ttft_ms) / 1000)
rows = []
for feature, g in ok.groupby("feature"):
    rows.append({"feature": feature, "calls": len(g),
                 "ttft p50": g.ttft_ms.median(), "ttft p95": g.ttft_ms.quantile(0.95),
                 "total p50": g.total_ms.median(), "total p95": g.total_ms.quantile(0.95),
                 "total p99": g.total_ms.quantile(0.99), "tokens/s": g.tokens_per_s.median()})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("feature").round(0).to_string())
cut = ok[ok.stop_reason == "max_tokens"]
print(f"responses cut off at max_tokens: {len(cut)} ({len(cut) / len(ok):.1%}), "
      f"median total {cut.total_ms.median():.0f} ms")
slow = ok[ok.total_ms > ok.total_ms.quantile(0.99)]
print(f"slowest 1%: {len(slow)} calls, median output {slow.output_tokens.median():.0f} tokens "
      f"vs {ok.output_tokens.median():.0f} overall")

"""Guardrail metrics: how often each guardrail fires, and how often it is right, from human review."""
import pandas as pd

log = pd.read_csv("usage_log.csv")
review = pd.read_csv("guardrail_review.csv")

print("block rate by feature:")
print(pd.crosstab(log.feature, log.guardrail, normalize="index").round(3).to_string())
refusals = (log.stop_reason == "refusal").sum()
print(f"model refusals (stop_reason refusal): {refusals} ({refusals / len(log):.2%})")

for name in ["blocked_input", "blocked_output"]:
    blocked = review[review.guardrail == name]
    precision = (blocked.human_label == "harmful").mean()
    print(f"{name}: {len(blocked)} reviewed, {precision:.0%} really harmful "
          f"(false positive share {1 - precision:.0%})")
allowed = review[review.guardrail == "allowed"]
missed = (allowed.human_label == "harmful").mean()
print(f"allowed sample: {len(allowed)} reviewed, {missed:.1%} harmful, "
      f"about {missed * (log.guardrail == 'allowed').sum():.0f} missed calls across the month")

hints: The usage fields follow the Messages API: input_tokens excludes cache writes and reads, which have their own fields and rates.
Costs are in invented course credits on purpose: the method matters here, not any provider's prices.
The missed-call estimate scales a sample rate to the month; say how uncertain it is (a Wilson interval on 4 of 300 is wide).

modules.title: Online feedback and A/B tests
modules.summary: Collect feedback that can be linked and trusted, run A/B tests of prompt and model changes with the right unit, size and checks, and keep evaluating after launch.

lessons.title: Feedback you can learn from
objectives: Combine explicit and implicit feedback signals
Link feedback to traces and versions and correct for its bias
key_points: Explicit feedback (thumbs, ratings, comments) is sparse and biased: few users rate and unhappy ones rate more often, so in the lab the thumbs-up share (59.4%) understates resolved conversations (62.7%).

Implicit signals cover every interaction: retrying or rephrasing, copying the answer, editing a draft before sending, abandoning, or escalating to a person; define each precisely and check it against real outcomes.
Store feedback with the trace ID, prompt and model versions and time, so it can be analysed per version and the exact request inspected.
Route samples to human review: every low rating, a random sample of the rest and new kinds of input, with a rubric reviewers apply consistently.
Close the loop: confirmed failures become golden-set cases, with consent and redaction, and the set is reweighted when the mix of real questions changes.

lessons.title: A/B testing LLM changes
objectives: Design an A/B test with the right unit, metrics and size
Analyse it with a sample ratio check and per-user statistics
key_points: Randomise by a stable unit, usually the user, with a salted hash of the user ID so each user sees one version; analyse per user too, because one user's conversations aren't independent.

Check the sample ratio first, with a chi-squared test of users per arm against the planned split: a mismatch (commonly p < 0.001) means broken assignment or logging, and no result should be read until it's fixed.

Pick one primary metric, such as the share of conversations resolved, plus guardrail metrics such as cost, latency and refusals: in the lab, B lifts resolution by 2.2 points (95% CI +0.5 to +3.9) but costs 12% more per conversation.
Size the test before it starts: detecting a change from 64% to 67% with 80% power at α = 0.05 needs about 3,940 users per arm, and smaller tests mostly measure noise.

Don't stop at the first p < 0.05: in the lab's A/A simulation, daily peeking raised false positives from 4.6% to 22.5%. Fix the duration in advance or use a sequential method built for repeated looks.

lessons.title: From experiment to continuous evaluation
objectives: Combine offline gates, staged rollout and online tests into one release process
Keep evaluating a live LLM feature after launch
key_points: Release in layers: the golden set and regression gate first, then a shadow or small canary, then the A/B test, with written criteria for moving on at each step.
Decide with every metric in view: a gain in the primary metric that costs more or answers more slowly needs an explicit trade-off made by the product owner, recorded with the evidence.
Watch for novelty and learning effects: users can react to change itself, so look at results over time within the test and keep a holdout group for long-running changes.
After launch, keep evaluating: run the golden set on a schedule against the live configuration, sample production for review and validate judges again when models change.
Record each decision with its versions, results and intervals, so later changes are compared with the reasons behind earlier ones.

files.content:
"""Simulate an A/B test of two prompt versions: users are assigned by a stable hash, have one to
three conversations each, and the logs record resolution, feedback, cost and latency."""
import argparse
import hashlib

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--users", type=int, default=8000)
parser.add_argument("--drop-b", type=float, default=0.0, help="simulate a logging bug losing B's users")
args = parser.parse_args()
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)


def arm(user_id, salt="support-prompt-test-1"):
    """Stable, independent of everything else about the user, and different for every experiment."""
    return "B" if int(hashlib.sha256(f"{salt}:{user_id}".encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % 2 else "A"


rows = []
for u in range(args.users):
    user = f"u{u:05d}"
    group = arm(user)
    if group == "B" and rng.random() < args.drop_b:
        continue                                          # the bug: these users never reach the logs
    skill = rng.normal(0, 0.6)                            # some users' questions are simply harder
    for _ in range(rng.integers(1, 4)):
        p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(0.5 + skill + (0.13 if group == "B" else 0.0))))
        resolved = rng.random() < p
        feedback = rng.random() < (0.10 if not resolved else 0.05)      # unhappy users rate more often
        rows.append({"user_id": user, "arm": group, "resolved": int(resolved),
                     "thumbs": ("up" if rng.random() < (0.3 if not resolved else 0.9) else "down") if feedback else "",
                     "cost": round(rng.gamma(4, 0.004) * (1.12 if group == "B" else 1.0), 5),
                     "latency_ms": round(rng.lognormal(7.6, 0.35) * (1.06 if group == "B" else 1.0))})
pd.DataFrame(rows).to_csv("experiment.csv", index=False)
print(f"wrote experiment.csv: {len(rows)} conversations from {len({r['user_id'] for r in rows})} users")

"""Analyse the A/B test: check the split, compare the primary metric per user (the unit that was
randomised), check guardrail metrics, and read feedback with its bias in mind."""
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_effectsize

log = pd.read_csv("experiment.csv")
users = log.groupby(["user_id", "arm"]).agg(resolved=("resolved", "mean"), cost=("cost", "mean"),
                                            conversations=("resolved", "size")).reset_index()

counts = users.arm.value_counts().reindex(["A", "B"])
srm = stats.chisquare(counts, [counts.sum() / 2] * 2)
print(f"users: A {counts['A']}, B {counts['B']}; sample ratio check p = {srm.pvalue:.2g}"
      + ("  <- MISMATCH: fix the pipeline before reading any result" if srm.pvalue < 0.001 else ""))

a, b = users[users.arm == "A"].resolved, users[users.arm == "B"].resolved
t = stats.ttest_ind(b, a, equal_var=False)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
boot = [rng.choice(b.values, len(b)).mean() - rng.choice(a.values, len(a)).mean() for _ in range(2000)]
print(f"resolution rate per user: A {a.mean():.3f}, B {b.mean():.3f}, difference {b.mean() - a.mean():+.3f} "
      f"(95% CI {np.percentile(boot, 2.5):+.3f} to {np.percentile(boot, 97.5):+.3f}, Welch p = {t.pvalue:.4f})")

for metric in ["cost", "latency_ms"]:
    ma, mb = log[log.arm == "A"][metric], log[log.arm == "B"][metric]
    stat = "mean" if metric == "cost" else "p95"
    va, vb = (ma.mean(), mb.mean()) if metric == "cost" else (ma.quantile(0.95), mb.quantile(0.95))
    print(f"guardrail {metric} ({stat}): A {va:.4g}, B {vb:.4g} ({vb / va - 1:+.1%})")

rated = log[log.thumbs != ""] if log.thumbs.dtype == object else log[log.thumbs.notna()]
print(f"feedback: {len(rated) / len(log):.1%} of conversations rated; thumbs up "
      f"{(rated.thumbs == 'up').mean():.1%} of ratings vs {log.resolved.mean():.1%} of all conversations resolved")

effect = proportion_effectsize(0.67, 0.64)
n = NormalIndPower().solve_power(effect_size=effect, alpha=0.05, power=0.8, ratio=1.0)
print(f"users per arm needed to detect 64% -> 67% with 80% power: {np.ceil(n):.0f}")

"""Why not to stop a test the first time p < 0.05: simulate A/A tests, where nothing differs."""
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
experiments, days, per_day = 1000, 14, 200
end_only = peeking = 0
for _ in range(experiments):
    a = rng.random((days, per_day)) < 0.6            # both arms convert at 60%: any "effect" is noise
    b = rng.random((days, per_day)) < 0.6
    p_values = []
    for d in range(1, days + 1):
        x, y = a[:d].ravel(), b[:d].ravel()
        p_values.append(stats.ttest_ind(x, y).pvalue)
    end_only += p_values[-1] < 0.05
    peeking += min(p_values) < 0.05
print(f"A/A tests: {experiments}, {days} daily looks, {per_day} users per arm per day")
print(f"false positives, one look at the end: {end_only / experiments:.1%}")
print(f"false positives, stopping at the first p < 0.05: {peeking / experiments:.1%}")

hints: analyse_ab.py averages each user's conversations first, because the user, not the conversation, was randomised.
peeking.py runs 1,000 simulated tests with 14 looks each and can take a minute.
A significant lift can still be the wrong thing to ship: the memo is about the whole trade-off.

study_plan.focus: Build the golden set and evaluation harness, and compare two versions pairwise.
Gate a prompt change with case-by-case regression, McNemar's test and replayed recordings.
Instrument the assistant with OpenTelemetry and analyse its traces.
Report cost, latency and guardrail quality from a month of usage logs.
Analyse an A/B test of two prompt versions and write the decision memo.
Build and submit the LLMOps capstone, then review with the mock exam and the flashcards.

project.title: Run LLMOps for a customer-support assistant
project.brief: Quillfern Homeware's support assistant is about to get a new prompt and possibly a new model, and the team wants to release changes like this safely and often. Build the LLMOps around it. Extend the golden set to at least 40 cases in at least five slices, with programmatic checks for every case and a rubric judge where checks can't reach; wire it into a regression gate with case-by-case diffs, McNemar's test, safety blockers and replayed recordings that run in pytest; instrument the assistant with OpenTelemetry spans using the GenAI conventions and analyse a batch of traces; report cost per feature and per successful task, latency percentiles and guardrail precision; and plan the A/B test for the change, with the unit, metrics, sample size and analysis, run on simulated data. Everything must run offline with recorded answers; live Claude calls are optional and read the model from CLAUDE_MODEL.
deliverables: The golden set (40 or more cases) with its slices, sources and version, and the harness that scores it
The regression gate: regression report, pytest suite with recordings, and the written gate policy
The traced assistant and a trace analysis: latency by span, retries, token use and blocked requests
A cost, latency and guardrail report with at least three alerts you would set
An A/B test plan and its analysis on simulated data, with a decision memo
A one-page runbook: releasing a prompt or model change from first evaluation to full rollout

rubric.name: Evaluation set and harness
rubric.description: Cases cover real, hard, incident and safety slices with clear pass rules; results are reported by slice with intervals; the judge is versioned, cached and validated.

rubric.name: Regression gate
rubric.description: Runs are compared case by case with a paired test, safety failures block, recordings make the suite deterministic, and the policy says when recordings are refreshed.

rubric.name: Tracing
rubric.description: Spans cover every step with GenAI attributes, content capture is justified, and the analysis explains latency, retries and token use without double counting.

rubric.name: Cost, latency and guardrails
rubric.description: Cost includes cache tokens, failures and per-success figures; latency is reported per feature with tails; guardrails are judged by reviewed precision and misses.

rubric.name: Online evaluation
rubric.description: The A/B plan randomises by user, is sized in advance, checks the sample ratio, analyses per user and weighs guardrail metrics in a clear decision.

project.submit: Paste a link to your repository (or the key files), the outputs of the harness, the gate, the trace analysis, the reports and the A/B analysis, and the runbook.
